note: Places where the gospels arrange the same event differently. Aland's sectional order follows the synoptic sequence; where John's placement diverges, the pericope says so rather than harmonizing silently.
25: John places this cleansing at the beginning of Jesus' ministry, at his first Passover in Jerusalem (John 2:13). The synoptics place a cleansing in the last week of his life (§273). Some readers take these as two separate acts, others as one act reported at different points in the narrative for different purposes — John opening his gospel with a claim on the temple, the synoptics making it the act that provokes the arrest.
273: Here the synoptics place the cleansing: in Holy Week, days before the arrest, as the act that hardens official opposition. John reported a cleansing three years earlier (§25). This column set therefore compares Matthew, Mark and Luke against a John passage held by many readers to describe a different occasion.
267: Matthew and Mark put this anointing two days before the Passover (Matt. 26:2; Mark 14:1), John six days before it (John 12:1), and John names the woman as Mary of Bethany. Luke 7:36–50 tells a similar story in Galilee, much earlier, with a different point. Aland prints the accounts together so the differences can be seen; he does not claim they are one occasion.
306: The anointing again, in Aland's Passion sequence. On the dating and the identity of the woman, see the note at §267.
308: The synoptics have the last supper as a Passover meal, eaten on the evening the lambs were killed (Mark 14:12; Luke 22:15). John has Jesus die while the lambs are being killed: the Jewish leaders have not yet eaten the Passover on the morning of the trial (John 18:28), and the crucifixion falls on the day of Preparation (John 19:14). Proposed resolutions include differing festival calendars, a Judaean-versus-Galilean reckoning of the day, and John's deliberate placing of the death at the hour of the lamb.
311: Whether this meal was the Passover itself turns on the same difference of reckoning described at §308. Read the synoptic accounts and John 13 side by side and note what each writer chooses to report about the meal — the synoptics the bread and cup, John the washing of feet.
344: Mark 15:25 puts the crucifixion at the third hour; John 19:14 has Jesus still before Pilate at about the sixth. Ancient timekeeping was approximate and reckoned from different starting points, and each writer marks the hours that serve his account. Treat the times as narrative markers rather than a clock reading.
